Mr. President, distinguished colleagues, the Russian Federation is the initiator of the process to develop the first international treaty in history on information security, hopes that there will be unanimous adoption by General Assembly of the UN of the draft Convention Against Cybercrime. This document is the outcome of 5 years of painstaking work by the part— on the part of UN member states since the adoption in 2019 of the resolution of the UNGA 74/247 establishing a special committee, and until the adoption of the draft of this treaty in August 2024. Negotiations were tense. Not all participants were constructively Certain countries tried to undermine the process and used dubious methods to do so. They exerted political pressure and to do so used certain tamed NGOs and companies to do so. And they even hindered full participation of the Russian delegation in the event through the ad hoc committee. In particular, Austria and the U.S. refused to to issue visas to heads of delegation, deputy heads, and experts, thus violating their obligations as host countries of UN offices and headquarters. Together with certain other delegations, they called for expanded participation of non-state actors in the work of the special— of the ad hoc committee, thus undermining intergovernmental, interstate, and negotiation process in the UN. This bad sportsmanship of these states also was shown in discussions of the Special Committee. Despite the adopted resolutions of the UNGA 74/247, the mandate of this UN body, that is to develop a comprehensive specialized international treaty, is something the Western countries actively promoted the human rights agenda in it. In their own interpretation of human rights, that's ignoring the aspirations and motivations of developing countries. The efforts of U.S. delegations and their allies caused the text to exclude a number of provisions on the use of ICT for terrorist and extremist purposes and how to prevent that, as well as illegal circulation of narcotics and weapons. As well as incitement to suicide or other dangerous forms of crimes, including attacks on critical ICT infrastructure. And modern methods of identification of ICT crimes were also left out of account— special investigation methods. And there are provisions left that could be used by interested states to withdraw from cooperation in combating ICT criminals. In this regard, the mandate of the ad hoc committee in accordance with Resolution 74/247 was only partially implemented. Russia, with reservations, adopted the August draft convention and reserves the right to make statements and to issue relevant reservations when signing and ratifying the convention. Despite the shortcomings in this text, the adopted treaty is a strong foundation for law enforcement cooperation to combat ICT crime. It is focused on fighting unsanctioned access to electronic data and their illegal seizure, as well as forgery and embezzlement or fraud, laundering ill-gotten revenue, exploitation of children, and harassment of these The document also allows for carrying out the main principle of the UN, that is protecting sovereignty, as well as exchange of electronic evidence, the functioning of a network of national contact centers for investigating crime 24/7. It establishes a permanent review body, the Conference of Member States— of State Parties. However, this universal treaty should not stand still. It needs to further evolve and improve, and this can be done by developing additional protocols. There's opportunities to criminalize the use of ICT for terrorist and extremist purposes. I'd like to also thank the Socialist Republic of Vietnam for the initiative of organizing a ceremonial signing of the Convention Against Cybercrime in Hanoi. We're prepared to provide partners with support in this event and hope to attract the largest possible number of participants. And we will encourage the UNODC to implement necessary assistance, including through Russian voluntary contributions to the budget of this body. We call on UN member states to go to Vietnam to sign this international treaty and ratify it immediately. The launch of mechanisms provided for by the Convention, we believe, will allow us to significantly combat information crime, the scale of which is exponentially growing. Thank you.
